items.question: Can good or bad deeds still bind the liberated person?
premises: The Ananta-verses state that good and bad deeds might be suspected as binding.
An objection arises that karma could still affect the liberated person.
The text answers that such binding would not occur for him.
items.inference: Even if karma is suspected as a bond, it does not bind the liberated person.
uncertainties: The exact source or identity of the Ananta-verses is not specified here.
items.plain_english: The Ananta-verses say that one might suspect good or bad deeds to bind him, but in fact they do not bind him.

rows.gloss: from the word 'even' with unlost memory
death only of one with lost memory

items.question: Does death with unlost memory change the liberated state?
premises: The word 'even' suggests the possibility of dying with memory intact.
Death is ordinarily associated with loss of memory.
If memory is lost before death, that condition is irrelevant to the liberated state.
items.inference: Whether memory is lost before death does not affect the liberation already attained.
uncertainties: The referent of 'that' in 'what use is that' could be memory-loss or the prior condition.
items.plain_english: From the word 'even' one might think death with memory intact is possible, but death usually involves lost memory; and if memory was lost before death, what does that matter?

rows.gloss: would be what is considered possible

items.question: What does the optative and time-expression indicate about death and liberation?
premises: The optative mood expresses possibility rather than certainty.
A time-expression in the text points to a temporal framing.
The text declares that death is not the cause of liberation.
items.inference: The grammatical form and time-expression show that death does not cause liberation.
uncertainties: The exact prior verse or phrase containing the optative and time-expression is not quoted.
items.plain_english: The optative indicates mere possibility, and the time-expression shows that death is not the cause of liberation.

rows.gloss: the body that had to be lived out
because of giving difference, even this

items.question: Why does the residual body not undermine sorrowless liberation?
premises: The term 'isolation' can raise doubt because a body still remains.
A remaining body might seem to produce difference.
That difference-producing power is destroyed in the liberated state.
items.inference: Because the body's power to produce difference is destroyed, sorrowlessness remains.
uncertainties: The precise sense of 'kaivalya' here may differ from classical Sāṃkhya usage.
items.plain_english: Although 'isolation' may raise doubt because a body remains, that body no longer produces difference, so sorrowlessness is established.

rows.gloss: connection with another body and so on

items.question: Does connection with one's own body differentiate the living-liberated person?
premises: Connection with other bodies does not differentiate the liberated person.
The living-liberated person still has a connection with his own body.
The analogy suggests the same non-differentiating status applies.
items.inference: For the living-liberated person, connection with his own body does not create differentiation.
items.plain_english: Just as connection with other bodies does not differentiate him, so too connection with his own body does not differentiate the living-liberated person.

rows.gloss: who has rejected all forms of the universe
of one not different from Śiva

items.question: Does embodiment or disembodiment make a difference for one non-different from Śiva?
premises: The liberated person has rejected identification with all universal forms.
He is non-different from Śiva.
Embodiment and disembodiment are presented as alternatives.
items.inference: For one non-different from Śiva, there is no essential difference between having a body and not having one.
items.plain_english: Therefore, for one who is non-different from Śiva and has set aside all universal forms, there is no real difference whether he is in a body or not.

rows.gloss: because of the persistence of suspicion from prior impressions of that difference
because of resorting to another measure

items.question: Why is the term 'aloneness' used despite non-difference from Śiva?
premises: Prior impressions may still give rise to suspicion of difference.
The text now speaks of aloneness.
Alternatively, the term may be used from another standpoint.
items.inference: The term 'aloneness' is used provisionally, either because old impressions of difference persist or because of another standpoint.
uncertainties: The phrase 'another measure' (mātrāntara) is somewhat ambiguous in this context.
items.plain_english: Even so, because suspicion based on old impressions of difference may persist, the text now speaks of aloneness; or else it does so from another standpoint.

rows.gloss: also stated in the revered Traiśirasa
free from the pair of sun and moon

items.question: How is liberation described in relation to non-difference and the Traiśirasa teaching?
premises: The liberated person is not known as different from things, nor they from him.
Such a person is called liberated.
The Traiśirasa scripture describes a state beyond the sun-moon pair.
items.inference: Liberation is the state of non-difference, as also taught in the Traiśirasa beyond dual channels.
uncertainties: The referent of 'those' (tāni) is not explicit in this verse alone.
items.plain_english: Those things do not know him as different, and he is not known as different by them; such a one is called liberated. The revered Traiśirasa also speaks of a state beyond the pair of sun and moon.

rows.gloss: abiding in the breaking of disgust and non-disgust
beyond valid cognition and mental constructs

items.question: What kind of awareness is described in the Traiśirasa state?
premises: The state transcends both disgust and its absence.
It is steady, all-pervasive, and free from calamity.
It goes beyond ordinary means of knowledge and mental constructs.
items.inference: The Traiśirasa describes a steady, transcendent awareness beyond dual reactions and ordinary cognition.
items.plain_english: It is a state where disgust and its opposite are broken, steady on all sides like a pillar, free from all calamity, and beyond valid cognition and mental constructs.

rows.gloss: though a doer of actions, unstained

items.question: How can one act yet remain unstained in that awareness?
premises: Absorption in inner awareness leaves the doer unstained by action.
The teaching uses the analogy of space inside a pot.
When the pot is broken, space is not destroyed.
items.inference: Like space unaffected by the pot, the self remains unstained by action in that awareness.
uncertainties: The form 'maṣṭe' is unusual and may reflect a textual or orthographic variant.
items.plain_english: Absorbed in that inner awareness, one may still act yet remain unstained. The key example is space in a pot: even when the pot is broken, space is not destroyed.

rows.gloss: would perish; just like that this self

items.question: What becomes of the self when the body perishes, according to the analogy?
premises: Space does not perish when the pot is broken.
The self is compared to that space.
The knower is established as independent and Śiva-natured.
items.inference: The self does not perish with the body but abides as Śiva and pervades all things.
items.plain_english: Just as space does not perish when the pot is broken, so this self does not perish; the knower becomes Śiva-natured, independent, and extends into all things.

rows.gloss: this very thing, O inner teacher
the teacher spoke in the Gītā

items.question: How is the liberated knower described beyond ordinary categories?
premises: The knower is not adequately described by being or non-being.
He is not confined to fixed form or mental construction.
This teaching is supported by what the teacher said in the Gītā.
items.inference: The liberated knower transcends the ordinary categories of existence, form, and conceptualization.
uncertainties: The vocative 'antarāgūrya' is difficult and may be a textual variant or rare address.
items.plain_english: For him there is neither mere being nor non-being, neither fixed form nor mental construction. This same point was spoken by the teacher in the Gītā.

rows.gloss: formed by dwelling on that state

items.question: What determines the state attained at the moment of leaving the body?
premises: At death a person remembers some state or object.
One attains the state one remembers at the end.
That remembrance is shaped by what one has continually dwelt on.
items.inference: The final remembered state, formed by lifelong habituation, determines what is attained at death.
items.plain_english: Whatever state one remembers while leaving the body at the end, that alone one attains, because one has always been shaped by dwelling on that state.

items.question: What practice and condition lead to an upward departure at death?
premises: One should remember the divine at all times while acting.
The state at death depends on prevailing qualities.
When sattva is dominant, the departing one goes upward.
items.inference: Constant remembrance together with dominant sattva leads to an upward departure.
items.plain_english: Therefore remember me at all times and fight. When sattva is predominant, the one who dissolves then goes upward.

rows.gloss: in sequence dissolved in rajas and tamas
going deluded into the womb of karma
confusion and being surrounded by labored breathing

items.question: What happens when rajas and tamas dominate at the time of death?
premises: Dominance of rajas and tamas leads to a different departure than sattva.
Such a person goes deluded into a karmic birth.
The dying state is marked by sensory confusion and labored breathing.
items.inference: When rajas and tamas prevail, death leads to deluded karmic rebirth accompanied by confusion and distress.
items.plain_english: If one dissolves in rajas and tamas, one goes deluded into a karmic birth; then there is confusion of the senses and distress marked by labored breathing.

rows.gloss: this experience of death and so on

items.question: What is the actual moment of abandoning the body?
premises: The experiences described above occur while still in the body.
These experiences are not themselves the abandonment of the body.
The true abandonment is a single final moment of breathing.
items.inference: Death-experiences occur in the body, but the real abandonment of the body is only the final breath-moment.
items.plain_english: Experiences like these occur in the body and are not the same as abandoning the body; the real abandonment is only that single final moment consisting of the last breath.

rows.gloss: becomes like wood or a wall
the fractional instant of the time of abandoning the body

items.question: How is the precise instant of separation from the body defined?
premises: After a certain final moment, the body becomes inert like wood or a wall.
That moment is a fractional instant in time.
It is the instant that actually separates one from the body.
items.inference: The abandonment of the body is defined as the tiny instant immediately before the body becomes inert.
items.plain_english: The instant immediately after which the body becomes like wood or a wall is the fractional moment of abandoning the body, the moment that separates one from it.

rows.gloss: devoid of that body's pleasure, pain, and so on
from the awakening of prior impressions

items.question: What is remembered at the moment of separation from the body?
premises: At that instant the person is no longer affected by the body's pleasure and pain.
Memory still operates at that moment.
What is remembered arises from awakened prior impressions.
items.inference: At the moment of separation, freed from bodily feeling, one remembers what prior impressions awaken.
items.plain_english: At that very moment, free from the body's pleasure and pain, one remembers whatever is awakened by prior impressions.

rows.gloss: caused by unseen merit, repeated practice, abundance, descent of power, and so on

items.question: Why does one attain a particular form at the moment of death?
premises: The remembered content is shaped by unseen factors, practice, intensity, and grace.
The dying person assumes the form corresponding to that remembrance.
That form may be characterized by pleasure, pain, or delusion.
items.inference: One attains the form determined by the dominant causes shaping final remembrance.
items.plain_english: Because of unseen merit, repeated practice, intensity, descent of power, and similar causes, one attains that very form, whether happy, suffering, or deluded.

rows.gloss: free from pleasure and pain and so on
or of the nature of bliss

items.question: Why might one attain a state beyond pleasure and pain or a state of bliss?
premises: Not all attained forms are marked by pleasure, pain, or delusion.
A state free from pleasure and pain or a blissful state is possible.
The attained state corresponds to what is remembered in consciousness.
items.inference: One attains a transcendent or blissful state because that is what is remembered in consciousness at the end.
items.plain_english: Or else, if one attains a state free from pleasure and pain, or one of bliss, why is that? Because that is what one remembers in consciousness.

rows.gloss: because of being established in consciousness

items.question: How does prior consciousness determine the body's experienced basis?
premises: What shone most strongly before becomes dominant.
The body is established through consciousness.
Consciousness functions by identifying with a prior basis.
items.inference: The dominant prior content becomes the body's basis because consciousness establishes it through identification.
items.plain_english: Whatever shone forth most strongly before becomes decisive, because this body is established in consciousness; what consciousness previously took as its basis through identification becomes that basis.

rows.gloss: in blue, yellow, and so on

items.question: What is meant by absorption in sattva, rajas, tamas, or knowable objects?
premises: Absorption is spoken of in relation to the guṇas and to knowable objects.
Consciousness takes up a previously constructed form.
That prior construction determines the mode of absorption.
items.inference: Absorption means consciousness taking up a previously constructed form within a guṇa or knowable object.
items.plain_english: This is what is called absorption in sattva, rajas, tamas, or in knowable things like blue and yellow: consciousness takes up a form that was previously constructed.

rows.gloss: therefore of what is merely to be established

items.question: How does consciousness make something into a lived basis rather than a mere object?
premises: Consciousness establishes a basis by taking its stand upon it.
Even a body can be treated as merely something established.
A wall is an example of a merely established object.
items.inference: Consciousness turns what is merely establishable into a lived basis, unlike an inert object such as a wall.
items.plain_english: Consciousness, by taking its stand, fully makes something into a basis; therefore, even if a body is something merely established, it differs from an inert thing like a wall.

rows.gloss: that it is prior to all that is to be established

items.question: What distinguishes the body from other objects established by consciousness?
premises: The body has a special status among things established by consciousness.
It is prior to all other objects that can be established.
Other things may also be identified with, but that identity is not known in the same way.
items.inference: The body is distinct because it serves as the primary basis for all further acts of establishment by consciousness.
uncertainties: The final clause is compressed and could also be read as emphasizing non-recognition of identity in other cases.
items.plain_english: The body is distinct because it comes first among all things that consciousness establishes. Other things may also be identified with, but that is not known in the same foundational way.
